claim: The large flight muscles of Drosophila develop from adult muscle progenitor (AMP) cells set-aside embryonically.
source: The large flight muscles of Drosophila develop from adult muscle progenitor (AMP) cells set-aside embryonically.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Currie and Bate, 1991; Fernandes et al., 1991; Roy and VijayRaghavan, 1999) in the introduction.

claim: The thoracic segments are all allotted the same small AMP number.
source: The thoracic segments are all allotted the same small AMP number, while those associated with the wing-disc proliferate extensively to give rise to over 2500 myoblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing approximately 10 AMPs in each thoracic segment at the end of embryogenesis.

claim: AMPs associated with the wing-disc proliferate extensively to give rise to over 2500 myoblasts.
source: The thoracic segments are all allotted the same small AMP number, while those associated with the wing-disc proliferate extensively to give rise to over 2500 myoblasts.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1 showing approximately 2500 Twi-positive cells at late third instar.

claim: An initial amplification of AMPs occurs through symmetric divisions.
source: An initial amplification occurs through symmetric divisions and is followed by a switch to asymmetric divisions in which the AMPs self-renew and generate post-mitotic myoblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by twin-spot MARCM experiments showing equal-sized clones in early larval stages (Figure 2A-C).

claim: AMPs switch to asymmetric divisions in which they self-renew and generate post-mitotic myoblasts.
source: An initial amplification occurs through symmetric divisions and is followed by a switch to asymmetric divisions in which the AMPs self-renew and generate post-mitotic myoblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by twin-spot MARCM experiments showing unequal-sized clones in third instar (Figure 2D-F).

claim: Notch signaling controls the initial amplification of AMPs.
source: Notch signaling controls the initial amplification of AMPs, while the switch to asymmetric division additionally requires Wingless, which regulates Numb expression in the AMP lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing reduced mitotic activity upon Notch downregulation (Figure 5D).

claim: The switch to asymmetric division additionally requires Wingless.
source: Notch signaling controls the initial amplification of AMPs, while the switch to asymmetric division additionally requires Wingless, which regulates Numb expression in the AMP lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing loss of Numb expression and symmetric divisions in Wg loss-of-function experiments (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Wingless regulates Numb expression in the AMP lineage.
source: Notch signaling controls the initial amplification of AMPs, while the switch to asymmetric division additionally requires Wingless, which regulates Numb expression in the AMP lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing complete loss of Numb expression in Wg loss-of-function experiments (Figure 8O-V).

claim: The epidermal tissue of the wing imaginal disc acts as a niche expressing the ligands Serrate and Wingless.
source: In both cases, the epidermal tissue of the wing imaginal disc acts as a niche expressing the ligands Serrate and Wingless.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunolabeling data showing Serrate and Wingless expression in the disc epithelium (Figures 6, 8).

claim: The disc-associated AMPs are a novel muscle stem cell population.
source: The disc-associated AMPs are a novel muscle stem cell population that orchestrates the early phases of adult flight muscle development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing self-renewal and generation of differentiated progeny through symmetric and asymmetric divisions.

claim: In each thoracic segment a total of approximately 10 cells were Twi-positive and dorsally located at the end of embryogenesis.
source: In each thoracic segment a total of approximately 10 cells were Twi-positive and dorsally located indicating that these correspond to the dorsal AMPs (Figure 1A) (Williams et al., 1991; Creig and Akam et al., 1993).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing Twi-positive cells in thoracic segments.

claim: Immediately after larval hatching (24 hr AEL) a total of 10 (±2) Twi-positive cells were found on the wing disc.
source: Immediately after larval hatching (24 hr AEL) a total of 10 (±2) Twi-positive cells were found on the wing disc implying that these had not yet initiated proliferative divisions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative data from Figure 1B.

claim: At the late second instar stage (72 hr AEL) the number of Twi-positive cells associated with the wing disc had increased to approximately 250 (±15).
source: At the late second instar stage (72 hr AEL) the number of Twi-positive cells associated with the wing disc had increased to approximately 250 (±15) and at the late third instar stage (144 hr AEL) approximately 2500 (±90) Twi-positive cells were found on the wing disc indicative of intense proliferative activity (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative data from Figure 1C-E.

claim: At the late third instar stage (144 hr AEL) approximately 2500 (±90) Twi-positive cells were found on the wing disc.
source: At the late second instar stage (72 hr AEL) the number of Twi-positive cells associated with the wing disc had increased to approximately 250 (±15) and at the late third instar stage (144 hr AEL) approximately 2500 (±90) Twi-positive cells were found on the wing disc indicative of intense proliferative activity (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative data from Figure 1C-E.

claim: Each embryonically born AMP gives rise to a lineage of approximately 250 cells during larval development.
source: These findings suggest that each embryonically born AMP, on the average, would give rise to a lineage of approximately 250 cells during larval development.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from the data showing 10 AMPs expanding to 2500 cells (2500/10 = 250).

claim: Twin-spot MARCM clones induced between the early first instar and the late second instar resulted in two relatively large, differentially labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size.
source: Twin-spot MARCM clones induced between the early first instar and the late second instar invariably resulted in two relatively large, differentially labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size and contained a similar number of cells (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A-C showing equal-sized twin-spot clones.

claim: Mitotically active cells in the AMP lineages divide symmetrically during early larval development (30 hr–72 hr AEL).
source: This indicates that mitotically active cells in the AMP lineages divide symmetrically during early larval development (30 hr–72 hr AEL).
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from twin-spot MARCM data showing equal-sized clones.

claim: Twin-spot MARCM clones induced during larval development from the early third instar (∼75 hr AEL) onward resulted in two differentially labeled daughter cell clones of different number of cells.
source: In contrast, twin-spot MARCM clones induced during larval development from the early third instar (∼75 hr AEL) onward always resulted in two differentially labeled daughter cell clones of different number of cells in each clone (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D-F showing unequal-sized twin-spot clones.

claim: One of the two daughter cell clones invariably comprised one large labeled cell with elongated morphology, whereas the other daughter cell clone contained up to 10 (±3) smaller cells.
source: Notably, one of the two daughter cell clones invariably comprised one large labeled cell with elongated morphology, whereas the other daughter cell clone contained up to 10 (±3) smaller cells.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D-F showing asymmetric clone composition.

claim: Mitotically active cells in the AMP lineages divide during the third larval instar stage (72 hr–144 hr AEL), with each stem cell giving rise to one stem cell through self-renewal as well as a sibling cell which could differentiate further.
source: This indicates that mitotically active cells in the AMP lineages have differential clonal potential and divide during the third larval instar stage (72 hr–144 hr AEL), with each stem cell giving rise to one stem cell through self-renewal as well as a sibling cell which could differentiate further.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from twin-spot MARCM data showing asymmetric clones.

claim: During the first and second larval instars, AMPs are located in a single monostratified layer adjacent to, and in contact with, the wing disc epithelium.
source: During the first and second larval instars, AMPs labeled with the Twi are located in a single monostratified layer adjacent to, and in contact with, the wing disc epithelium (Figure 3A,B,B′).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A,B,B' showing monostratified arrangement.

claim: From the early third larval instar onward, labeled cells become organized in multistratified 2-3 cell layers on the wing disc.
source: From the early third larval instar onward, labeled cells become organized in multistratified 2-3 cell layers on the wing disc (Figure 3C,C′; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C,C' and Video 1 showing multistratified arrangement.

claim: Throughout larval development, PH3 positive cells were only observed in the cell layer immediately adjacent to the wing disc epithelium.
source: Throughout larval development, PH3 positive cells were only observed in the cell layer immediately adjacent to the wing disc epithelium.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D-D'' showing PH3 positive cells only in the proximal layer.

claim: Even in the multistratified organization manifested in the third larval instar, PH3 positive cells were seen only in cells located adjacent to the epithelium and not in cells located in more distal layers.
source: Notably, even in the multistratified organization manifested in the third larval instar, PH3 positive cells were seen only in cells located adjacent to the epithelium and not in cells located in more distal layers (Figure 3D–D″).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D-D'' showing PH3 positive cells only in the proximal layer.

claim: Almost all mitotically active cells are located proximal to the disc epithelium, while the cells in the more distal layers are likely to be postmitotic.
source: This implies that almost all mitotically active cells are located proximal to the disc epithelium, while the cells in the more distal layers are likely to be postmitotic.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from PH3 labeling data showing mitotic activity only in the proximal layer.

claim: Both symmetric and asymmetric cell divisions only take place in cells located adjacent to the wing disc epithelium.
source: Taken together with the findings on cell division modes in the AMP lineages, these results also suggest that both symmetric and asymmetric cell divisions only take place in cells located adjacent to the wing disc epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from combining twin-spot MARCM data with PH3 labeling data.

claim: Throughout the second instar stage, the axis of cell division in the mitotically active cells is oriented parallel to the surface of the wing disc epithelium.
source: Throughout the second instar stage, the axis of cell division in the mitotically active cells is oriented parallel to the surface of the wing disc epithelium such that both daughter cells remain in contact with the epithelium (Figure 3E–H′).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E-H' showing parallel division axis.

claim: From early third instar stage onward, the axis of cell division shows an oblique to orthogonal orientation relative to the disc surface.
source: In contrast, from early third instar stage onward, the axis of cell division shows an oblique to orthogonal orientation relative to the disc surface (Figure 3I–L′).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3I-L' showing oblique/orthogonal division axis.

claim: Only one of the two daughter cells remains in contact with the disc epithelium while the other daughter cell loses epithelial contact in third instar divisions.
source: Consequently, only one of the two daughter cells remains in contact with the disc epithelium while the other daughter cell loses epithelial contact and, hence, might contribute to the population of cells located in layers distal to the disc epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from the oblique/orthogonal division axis observed in third instar.

claim: When cells were examined directly after EdU incorporation (pulse, no chase), labeling was only found in cells adjacent to the disc epithelium.
source: When cells were examined directly after EdU incorporation (pulse, no chase), labeling was only found in cells adjacent to the disc epithelium (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A,B showing EdU labeling only in proximal cells.

claim: After EdU incorporation followed by 48 hr without EdU (pulse, chase), the majority of labeled cells were in the most distal layer.
source: If the incorporation of EdU was followed by 48 hr without EdU (pulse, chase) and the cells then examined, labeling was seen in all layers. However, in this case, the majority of labeled cells were in the most distal layer, less labeled cells were in an intermediate layer and the lowest number of labeled cells was found in the layer adjacent to the disc (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C,D showing EdU labeling predominantly in distal layers after chase.

claim: The cells in the more distal layers are the postmitotic progeny of the proliferating cells that remain in contact with the disc epidermis.
source: This, in turn, implies that the cells in the more distal layers are the postmitotic progeny of the proliferating cells that remain in contact with the disc epidermis.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from EdU pulse-chase experiments showing labeled cells moving to distal layers.

claim: MARCM clones induced in the second larval stage and recovered in the third larval stage typically comprised 100–200 labeled cells arranged in a loose cluster.
source: MARCM clones induced in the second larval stage and recovered in the third larval stage typically comprised 100–200 labeled cells arranged in a loose cluster and extending from the layer next to the disc epithelium to the most distal layer of cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E showing MARCM clone composition.

claim: Within each MARCM clone the labeled cells in the distal layer were larger in size and had a more elongated morphology than those located in the innermost layer next to the disc.
source: Interestingly, within each clone the labeled cells in the distal layer were larger in size and had a more elongated morphology than those located in the innermost layer next to the disc (Figure 4G–N; Video 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G-N and Video 2 showing size differences.

claim: Only one cell within the MARCM clone was PH3-positive and this cell was always located adjacent to the disc epithelium.
source: In all cases in which co-labeling was seen, only one cell within the clone was PH3-positive and this cell was always located adjacent to the disc epithelium (Figure 4F,F′; Video 3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4F,F' and Video 3 showing single PH3-positive cell in proximal position.

claim: All of the Twi-positive cells are co-immunolabeled by the anti-NICD antibody.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis shows that all of the Twi-positive cells are co-immunolabeled by the anti-NICD antibody (Figure 5A–C,F–H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A-C,F-H showing co-localization of Twi and NICD.

claim: NICD co-immunolabeling with Twi was seen in all larval instar stages and in all myogenic cell layers associated with the wing disc.
source: This co-immunolabeling was seen in all larval instar stages and in all myogenic cell layers associated with the wing disc.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by immunolabeling data.

claim: Down-regulation of Notch in AMPs resulted in a significant reduction in the number of mitotically active cells in late third instar stage.
source: A significant reduction in the number of mitotically active cells was observed; in the third instar stage only half the number of PH3-positive cells were seen in knockdown vs control experiments (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5D showing quantification of PH3-positive cells.

claim: Both the number and the layered organization of the ensemble of Twi-positive cells on the wing disc were reduced in Notch knockdown experiments.
source: Both the number and the layered organization of the ensemble of Twi-positive cells on the wing disc were reduced in these knockdown experiments (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5I-K showing reduced cell layers.

claim: Overexpression of an activated form of Notch in the AMP revealed a marked increase in mitotically active cells.
source: Conversely, overexpression of an activated form of N in the AMP using Dmef2-Gal 4 to drive UAS-NICD in second and third larval instar stages revealed a marked increase in mitotically active cells as assayed in late third instar stage. In these experiments the number of PH3-positive cells in the overexpression experiments was approximately twice as large as in controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5E showing quantification of PH3-positive cells.

claim: Both the number and the layered organization of the Twi-positive cells on the disc were increased in Notch overexpression experiments.
source: Correspondingly, both the number and the layered organization of the Twi-positive cells on the disc were increased in these overexpression experiments (Figure 5L–N).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 5L-N showing increased cell layers.

claim: In Notch overexpression experiments, mitotically active cells were occasionally seen in more distal cell layers.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to wild type controls, mitotically active cells were occasionally seen in more distal cell layers in N overexpression experiments (data not shown).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: Proliferative activity in the AMP lineages during larval development is dependent on Notch signaling.
source: These findings indicate that proliferative activity in the AMP lineages during larval development is dependent on N signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from Notch knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: Notch signaling acts to effect proliferation in the AMPs in the layer adjacent to the wing disc.
source: Since mitotic activity in the wild type is only seen in the layer of cells adjacent to the wing disc this further implies that N signaling acts to effect proliferation in the AMPs in this layer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from combining Notch signaling data with PH3 localization data.

claim: Serrate expression in the disc epithelium occurs in close proximity to AMPs in the adjacent myogenic cell layer.
source: Immunocytochemical labeling of the wing disc epithelium (with anti-DCad2) and of the AMP lineages (with anti-Twi) together with a Ser-specific marker (Ser-LacZ) reveals a close apposition of Ser-expressing wing disc cells and the AMP cell layer immediately adjacent to the disc epithelium (Figure 6A–H′; Video 4).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A-H' and Video 4 showing Serrate localization.

claim: This close apposition of Serrate-expressing cells and AMPs was observed in all larval stages.
source: This close apposition was observed in all larval stages.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by immunolabeling data.

claim: Knockdown of Serrate specifically in the dorsal wing disc region resulted in a marked reduction in the number of mitotically active AMPs.
source: A marked reduction in the number of mitotically active cells was observed; in the third instar stage less than half the number of PH3-positive cells were seen in knockdown vs control experiments (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 6I showing quantification of PH3-positive cells.

claim: The Serrate located in the wing disc epithelium is required for the mitotic activity of cells in the adjacent AMP layer.
source: These results indicate that the Ser located in the wing disc epithelium is required for the mitotic activity of cells in the adjacent AMP layer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from Serrate knockdown experiments showing reduced mitotic activity.

claim: Epithelial Serrate serves as a ligand for the activation of Notch receptor-mediated signaling in the myogenic AMP lineages.
source: Given the concomitant requirement of N for mitotic activity of these cells, this implies that epithelial Ser serves as a ligand for the activation of N receptor-mediated signaling in the myogenic AMP lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from combining Serrate and Notch requirement data.

claim: The Serrate-expressing cells in the wing disc epithelium represents a transient signaling niche for Notch activation of AMP proliferation.
source: This in turn suggests that the Ser-expressing cells in the wing disc epithelium represents a transient signaling niche for N activation of AMP proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from the spatial relationship between Serrate-expressing epithelium and proliferating AMPs.

claim: Numb is expressed in AMP lineages during the third instar stage but not in the two preceding larval stages.
source: These experiments show that Nb is expressed in AMP lineages during the third instar stage but not in the two preceding larval stages (data not shown).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: Throughout the third instar stage, Numb is expressed in all of the myogenic cells on the wing disc, however expression is strongest in the cells of the more distal layers and relatively weak in the cells adjacent to the disc epithelium.
source: Throughout the third instar stage, Nb is expressed in all of the myogenic cells on the wing disc, however expression is strongest in the cells of the more distal layers and relatively weak in the cells adjacent to the disc epithelium; this contrasts with N expression which is more uniformly distributed in all of these cell layers (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7A-D showing differential Numb expression.

claim: Numb might be required for the transition to asymmetric cell divisions in AMP lineages.
source: The fact that Nb is not expressed in AMP lineages during their symmetric division phase, but is present in these cells during their asymmetric division phase suggests that Nb might be required for the transition to asymmetric cell divisions in AMP lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from the temporal correlation between Numb expression and asymmetric divisions.

claim: Twin-spot MARCM clones with Numb knockdown induced in the early third instar stage consisted of two relatively large, differentially labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size and cell number indicative of symmetric divisions.
source: These twin-spot MARCM clones invariably consisted of two relatively large, differentially (RFP and GFP) labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size and cell number indicative of symmetric divisions (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7F-H showing symmetric clones.

claim: In the absence of Numb, cell divisions in AMP lineages are symmetric and not asymmetric in the third instar stage.
source: This indicates that in the absence of Nb, cell divisions in AMP lineages are symmetric and not asymmetric in the third instar stage, implying that Nb expression is necessary for the transition from the symmetric to the asymmetric division mode manifest in the third instar.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from twin-spot MARCM experiments with Numb knockdown.

claim: Twin-spot MARCM clones with constitutive Notch activation induced in the early third instar stage consisted of two relatively large, differentially labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size and cell number indicating a symmetric division mode.
source: Clones induced in the early third instar stage and recovered in the late third instar stage again consisted of two relatively large, differentially labeled daughter cell clones that were similar in size and cell number indicating a symmetric division mode (Figure 7I–K).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7I-K showing symmetric clones.

claim: Numb, through downregulation of Notch, is required for asymmetric proliferative divisions in the AMP lineages.
source: Since both downregulation of Nb and constitutive upregulation of N lead to continued symmetric cell divisions in the third instar stage, we postulate that Nb, through downregulation of N, is required for asymmetric proliferative divisions in the AMP lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from combining Numb knockdown and Notch overexpression data.

claim: During larval development of the wing disc, Wingless is expressed in the prospective wing blade region in all instar stages.
source: During larval development of the wing disc, Wg is expressed in the prospective wing blade region in all instar stages, however, expression in the prospective notum region, in which the developing AMP lineages reside, is only manifest from the early third instar onwards (Phillips and Whittle, 1993; Tomoyasu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wingless expression in the prospective notum region is only manifest from the early third instar onwards.
source: During larval development of the wing disc, Wg is expressed in the prospective wing blade region in all instar stages, however, expression in the prospective notum region, in which the developing AMP lineages reside, is only manifest from the early third instar onwards (Phillips and Whittle, 1993; Tomoyasu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Throughout the third instar stage, notal Wingless expression is seen in a stripe of epithelial cells that are closely apposed to the adjacent population of Twi positive cells.
source: Throughout the third instar stage, notal Wg expression is seen in a stripe of epithelial cells that are closely apposed to the adjacent population of Twi positive cells (Figure 8A–H; Video 5).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8A-H and Video 5 showing Wingless localization.

claim: Notal Wingless loss-of-function resulted in complete loss of beta-catenin activity in all Twi-positive cells.
source: In these experiments, notal Wg loss-of-function resulted in complete loss of beta-catenin activity in all Twi-positive cells implying that inductive Wg signaling from the notum region of the wing disc affects all myogenic cells in the third larval instar (Figure 8I–N).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8I-N showing loss of beta-catenin.

claim: Inductive Wingless signaling from the notum region of the wing disc affects all myogenic cells in the third larval instar.
source: In these experiments, notal Wg loss-of-function resulted in complete loss of beta-catenin activity in all Twi-positive cells implying that inductive Wg signaling from the notum region of the wing disc affects all myogenic cells in the third larval instar (Figure 8I–N).
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from beta-catenin loss in all Twi-positive cells upon Wingless loss-of-function.

claim: Wingless loss-of-function in the wing disc notum resulted in complete loss of Numb expression in all Twi-positive cells.
source: Wg loss-of-function in the wing disc notum resulted in complete loss of Nb expression in all Twi-positive cells (Figure 8O–V).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 8O-V showing loss of Numb expression.

claim: Wingless signaling in the wing disc notum is required for induction and maintenance of Numb expression in the myogenic AMP lineages in the third larval instar stage.
source: We conclude that Wg signaling in the wing disc notum is required for induction and maintenance of Nb expression in the myogenic AMP lineages in the third larval instar stage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from Wingless loss-of-function experiments showing loss of Numb.

claim: Notal Wingless loss-of-function results in the reduction of mitotic activity in the AMP lineages.
source: In addition to its effects on Nb expression, notal Wg loss-of-function also results in the reduction of mitotic activity in the AMP lineages. Thus, both the number of PH3 positive cells and the extent of the multilayered organization are reduced in Wg downregulation compared to wild type (Figure 9A–J, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 9A-J and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Down-regulation of Wingless prevents the switch in cell-division orientation from parallel to the epithelium to perpendicular to the epithelium.
source: The axis of the division in this background is parallel to the epithelium, similar to that seen in the early instars (Figure 9—figure supplement 2). Wg, in the presumptive notum is expressed only from the late second instar (Alexandre et al., 2014), therefore this result shows that down-regulation of Wg prevents the switch in cell-division orientation from parallel to the epithelium to perpendicular to the epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 2 showing parallel division axis upon Wingless downregulation.

claim: Wingless signaling from the wing disc niche might have dual effects on neighboring myogenic cells, namely the induction of Numb expression and the regulation of proliferation.
source: This suggests that Wg signaling from the wing disc niche might have dual effects on neighboring myogenic cells, namely the induction of Nb expression and the regulation of proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and inferred from the multiple effects of Wingless loss-of-function.

claim: The AMPs are lineal descendants of progenitor cells, derived from proneural gene-expressing equivalent groups in the embryonic mesoderm.
source: AMPs are lineal descendants of progenitor cells, derived from proneural gene-expressing equivalent groups in the embryonic mesoderm (Ruiz-Gómez and Bate, 1997; Carmena et al., 1998).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the thoracic segments of the embryo, each progenitor cell divides asymmetrically to generate a muscle founder cell involved in embryonic myogenesis and an AMP which has active Notch signaling and continues to express the mesodermal marker Twist.
source: In the thoracic segments of the embryo, each of these progenitor cells divides asymmetrically to generate a muscle founder cell involved in embryonic myogenesis and an AMP which has active Notch (N) signaling and continues to express the mesodermal marker Twist (Twi).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and represents established knowledge about AMP development.

claim: The AMPs do not differentiate in the embryo; rather they are set aside and at the end of embryonic development become associated with the imaginal discs.
source: In contrast to their muscle founder cell siblings, the AMPs do not differentiate in the embryo; rather they are set aside and at the end of embryonic development become associated with the imaginal discs (Bate et al., 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Twi-expressing AMPs associated with the wing imaginal discs co-express Vestigial in late embryonic stages.
source: The Twi-expressing AMPs associated with the wing imaginal discs co-express Vestigial (Vg) in late embryonic stages (Sudarsan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Stem cells populations can expand exponentially through symmetric division or asymmetrically divide to self-renew and produce a daughter cell, which differentiates to contribute to tissue formation or regeneration.
source: Stem cells populations can expand exponentially through symmetric division or asymmetrically divide to self-renew and produce a daughter cell, which differentiates to contribute to tissue formation or regeneration (Morrison and Kimble, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Mandal et al., 2007; Maurange et al., 2008; Knoblich, 2001; Egger et al., 2008; Doe, 2008; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2010; Brand and Livesey, 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Many mature tissues such as colon, prostate, lung, muscle and brain use adult-specific stem cells in tissue maintenance or regeneration.
source: Many mature tissues such as colon, prostate, lung, muscle and brain use adult-specific stem cells in tissue maintenance or regeneration (Reya et al., 2001; Gonzalez, 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The regulation of stem-cell proliferation is usually through signals from a 'stem-cell niche'.
source: The regulation of stem-cell proliferation is usually through signals from a 'stem-cell niche' (Mandal et al., 2007; Brack et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2012; Cordero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the developing optic lobe, stem cell-like neuroepithelial cells first increase in number through symmetric divisions and are then transformed into neuroblasts which undergo self-renewing asymmetric divisions.
source: For example, in the developing optic lobe, stem cell-like neuroepithelial cells first increase in number through symmetric divisions and are then transformed into so-called neuroblasts which undergo self-renewing asymmetric divisions to generate differentiated neurons and glial cells in this part of the brain (Maurange et al., 2008; Egger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila flight muscles are formed from adult muscle precursors (AMPs).
source: Drosophila flight muscles are formed from adult muscle precursors (AMPs) (Currie and Bate, 1991; Fernandes et al., 1991; Roy and VijayRaghavan, 1999).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myogenesis occurs in two phases; an embryonic one, which makes the muscles required for the larval life while a postembryonic phase leads to formation of muscle required for the adult.
source: Myogenesis occurs in two phases; an embryonic one, which makes the muscles required for the larval life (Bate et al., 1991) while a postembryonic phase leads to formation of muscle required for the adult (Fernandes et al., 1991; Roy and VijayRaghavan, 1998; Sudarsan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The AMPs, lineal derivatives of the mesoderm, are generated embryonically and proliferate postembryonically.
